titles.98: Hexades Prooemium H.I: Midway in the second millennium, is Reformation itself or its necessity more to be remembered?
titles.99: Head and members alike mourned the need to reform — ruined councils, Lateran barkers, and later historians prove it
titles.100: Zwingli and Luther openly pressed a Reformation long secretly begun — the indulgence market drove them
titles.101: §.II: Tetzel sold pardons under Wimpina in our own Viadrina — Luther posted theses at Wittenberg
titles.102: Against Leo's leonine teeth Luther burned the condemning bull and appealed to Charles V
titles.103: §.III: From Worms to the Augsburg Diet of 1530 Spanheim takes the Controversiae we now treat

latin.98:
HEXAS ANNOTATIONUM AD B. SPANHEMII PROTHEORIAM HISTORICAM ET CATALLACTICAM PRAECIPUARUM CONTROVERSIARUM CUM AUGUSTANAE CONFESSIONIS, UT VOCANTUR, THEOLOGIS.

Prooemium.
H. I.

Seculum decimum quintum, Secundi Millennii, inde à Christo nato, ad Seculorum omnium consummationem, communiori Doctorum, Eliam quempiam Judaeum sequentium, opinione, expectandi Medium (ad quod tum Elenchi Auctoris, tum nostra, Protheoria Historico-Catallactica pertinet) num Reformatione Christianismi ipsâ, an Reformationis Necessitate, per cuncta adhuc secutura Secula, commemorandum magis sit, in ambiguo propemodùm positum arbitramur.
latin.99: Necessitatem Reformationis in Capite Ecclesiae Christianae, (per insignem licèt abusum sic dictô) perinde atque in membris, uti istius temporis Status Christianorum omnes, tàm Spirituales, quàm Temporales, maximè ex Germanis & Gallis, & agnoverunt distinctè, & gravissimè doluerunt, quin profligatissimae Doctrinae pariter atque Vitae Papis, Juliis, Alexandris, Leonibus (post elusa ab his suique similibus elisaque, imò protrita planè ac conculcata Concilia saluberrima, Basiliense, Constantiense, Pisanum denique, Mediolani continuatum, Lugduni verò in Galliis confectum, idque per mille fraudes artesque malas, Concilia etiam opposita, mordaciter satis latrantia, i.e. Lateranensia potissimùm, aliaque lateritia à se habita) supplicibus passim de emendando precibus, partim acrioribus minis inculcarunt; ita hujus quoque aetatis, Viri per Orbem celeberrimi Reformationisque praeclarissimae, Dei gratiâ impetratae, participes, ex Reformatis in specie sic dictis ὁ πάνυ Hottingerus, tam in Historia Ecclesiastica, Parte V. & VI. quàm in Analectis Historico-Theologicis, Dissert. I. à pag. 1. ad 82. ex aliis Evangelicis, post Chytraeum & Celestinum, in Historiarum suarum Augustanae Confessionis Exordiis, etiam illustris Seckendorfius in Lutheranismo adversus Majemburgum defenso, Baclerus in Memoriali de rebus gestis Seculi XVI. p. 263. & seqq. & novissimè Celebris nominis Theologus Ulmensis, Dominus Elias Viel, peculiari Tractatu, pluribus expositum dederunt.
latin.100: Reformationem verò ipsam, multis jam retrò Seculis occultiùs inchoatam fotamque (quô de multi multa, ex professo Auctor Catalogi Testium Veritatis & Magnus Usserius Armachanus in aureo de Successione Ecclesiarum Libello) apertiùs, Deo duce, aggressi sunt in superiori alter, alter in inferiori Germania, Ulricus Zwinglius, & Martinus Lutherus; iste publicè docendô & contra papales doctrinas detonandô prior; hic easdem & scriptis & factis publicis variis prior impetendô impugnandóque; uterque, per impudentissimam cumprimis Indulgentiarum Papalium nundinationem, cui isthìc Samsonius quispiam, hic famosus Tezelius obstetricabantur, ad id pertractus, vid. Gerhard. Theod. Mejerum, Hist. Relig. Cap. V. §. 29. p. m. 253. 254.
latin.101:
§. II.
Tezelius quò efferatiùs, in hac ipsâ Viadrinâ nostrâ, sub umbone primi Academiae Rectoris Conradi Wimpinae, merces suas & venùm exponebat, & expositas commendabat, (absolutionem unicuique à scelere quovis pollicitus, qui vel decem solidos solvisset, & animarum ex Purgatorio Liberationem, simul ac contributio in Cistam conjiceretur, quin veniae impetrationem, etiamsi, per impossibilia, ipsam Dei Matrem violasset, referente Luthero in Epist. ad Archiepiscopum Moguntinum Albertum Brandenburgicum, Tom. I. Jenen. Latino, fol. 2.;) Eò animosiùs Luthero oppugnabatur, Wittenbergae ad valvas Templi, Theses suas contra foedam Indulgentiarum nundinationem affigendas curante.
latin.102: etiam Papae Leoni, sibi post plures, licèt humillimas factas deprecationes & protestationes (Tomo. I. Jen. Lat. fol. 69. in fine, & fol. 192. 210. in fine, fol. denique 435. legendas,) iniquiori ac leoninis prorsùs dentibus infestanti, tandem nunciùm mittente, combustâ Papali Bullâ condemnatoriâ, factâque ad Caesarem Carolum V. provocatione, Tom. II. Wittenb. Lat. fol. 44. & 45.
latin.103:
§. III.
Ea propter Caesaris hujus Auctoritate, initiò quidem Lutherus, Wormatiam, Anno 1521. fide publicâ evocatus est, ut palinodiam cantaret; at postremò, cùm citra praeviam errorum suorum ab adversariis, ex Scripturis Sacris, factam demonstrationem, Lutherus se recantaturum constantissimè abnuisset, Saxoniae quoque Dux & Elector, Divus Fridericus, cum aliis nonnullis Imperii Romano-Germanici Statibus, Doctrinae Lutheri propiùs accessisset, ab eodem Caesare Comitia Augustana ista ipsâ indicta, ac Anno 1530. Mense Julio (Luthero intereà Coburgi, ob periculi metum, commorante, uti refert Sleidanus Lib. VII.) celebrata sunt, à quibus Auctori nostro B. Spanhemio, in Elencho suo, praecipuae quaedam Controversiae cum Augustanae Confessionis, ut vocantur, Theologis, i.e. Controversiae a nobis pertractandae, inscribuntur.

pass_a.98: Hexades of Annotations on the blessed Spanheim's historical and reconciling Protheoria of the chief controversies with the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, as they are called. Prooemium. H. I. We judge it almost set in ambiguity whether the Middle of the second Millennium — from Christ's birth to the consummation of all ages — that is to be expected by the more common opinion of the learned who follow some Jewish Elijah (to which both the Elenchus-author's and our own Historico-Catallactic Protheoria belong) is more to be commemorated, through all ages still to follow, by the Reformation of Christianity itself, or by the Necessity of Reformation.
pass_a.99: The Necessity of Reformation in the Head of the Christian Church (so called, though by a notable abuse) as well as in the members — as all the Christian Estates of that time, spiritual and temporal, especially among Germans and French, both distinctly acknowledged and most heavily mourned, and indeed by humble prayers everywhere for amendment, and partly by sharper threats, pressed it home against the utterly ruined doctrine and life of the Popes Julius, Alexander, and Leo (after the most wholesome councils — Basel, Constance, and finally Pisa, continued at Milan and finished at Lyons in France — had been eluded, crushed, and even plainly trampled by them and their like through a thousand frauds and evil arts, and after opposite councils that barked mordantly enough, namely the Lateran ones above all and other brickish ones they held for themselves) — so also men of this age, world-famous and sharers in the most excellent Reformation obtained by God's grace, have set it out at length: among those specially called Reformed, the great Hottinger (ὁ πάνυ), both in Ecclesiastical History Parts V and VI and in the Historico-Theological Analecta, Dissertation I, pages 1–82; among other Evangelicals, after Chytraeus and Celestine in the openings of their histories of the Augsburg Confession, also the illustrious Seckendorf in Lutheranism defended against Maimbourg, Baclerus in the Memorial of sixteenth-century affairs, p. 263 and following, and most recently the celebrated Ulm theologian Elias Viel in a special treatise.
pass_a.100: But the Reformation itself, already more secretly begun and fostered through many ages past (on which many have said much, notably the author of the Catalog of Witnesses of the Truth and the great Ussher of Armagh in his golden booklet on the Succession of the Churches), was more openly undertaken under God's lead in upper and lower Germany by Ulrich Zwingli and Martin Luther — the former earlier in public teaching and thundering against papal doctrines; the latter earlier in attacking and assaulting the same by various public writings and deeds; both drawn to it chiefly by the most shameless trafficking in papal Indulgences, midwifed here by some Samsonius and there by the infamous Tetzel — see Gerhard Theodor Mejer, History of Religion, ch. V, §29, pp. 253–254.
pass_a.101: §. II. The more furiously Tetzel, in this very Viadrina of ours, under the shield of the Academy's first Rector Conrad Wimpina, exposed his wares for sale and praised them once exposed (promising everyone absolution from any crime who had paid even ten shillings, and liberation of souls from Purgatory as soon as the contribution was thrown into the chest, and even the obtaining of pardon though — by impossibles — he had violated God's own Mother, as Luther reports in the Letter to Archbishop Albert of Brandenburg of Mainz, Jena Latin Tom. I, fol. 2), the more boldly he was opposed by Luther, who had his Theses against that foul Indulgence-traffic affixed to the temple doors at Wittenberg.
pass_a.102: and who at last, when Pope Leo — the more unjust and with truly leonine teeth hostile to him after several most humble deprecations and protests had been made (to be read in Jena Latin Tom. I, fol. 69 at the end, and fol. 192, 210 at the end, and finally fol. 435) — sent him a message, burned the papal condemning Bull and made an appeal to Emperor Charles V (Wittenberg Latin Tom. II, fol. 44 and 45).
pass_a.103: §. III. For that reason, by this Emperor's authority, Luther was at first summoned under safe-conduct to Worms in 1521 to sing a palinode; but at last, when without any prior demonstration of his errors from Holy Scripture by his adversaries Luther most steadfastly refused to recant, and when also the Duke and Elector of Saxony, the divine Frederick, with some other Estates of the Romano-German Empire, had drawn nearer to Luther's doctrine, by the same Emperor those very Augsburg Diets were called and celebrated in July 1530 (Luther meanwhile staying at Coburg for fear of danger, as Sleidan reports in Book VII) — from which our author the blessed Spanheim, in his Elenchus, titles certain chief Controversies with the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, as they are called — that is, the Controversies to be treated by us.

98: HEXAS OF ANNOTATIONS on the blessed Spanheim's historical and reconciling Protheoria of the chief controversies with the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, as they are called.

We judge it nearly an open question whether the middle stretch of the second millennium — from Christ's birth to the end of all ages — that learned men who follow some Jewish Elijah more commonly expect (the stretch to which both the Elenchus-writer's Protheoria and our own historical-reconciling Protheoria belong) is better remembered, through every age still to come, by Christianity's Reformation itself, or by the necessity of Reformation.
99: The necessity of reforming the Christian Church in her head (so named, though by a striking abuse) as well as in her members was something every Christian estate of that age — spiritual and temporal, Germans and French above all — both saw clearly and mourned with heavy grief.

They pressed for amendment by humble prayers everywhere, and partly by sharper threats, against the utterly wrecked teaching and life of Popes Julius, Alexander, and Leo — after those men and their like had dodged, crushed, and even trampled the most wholesome councils (Basel, Constance, and at last Pisa, continued at Milan and finished at Lyons in France) by a thousand frauds and foul arts, and after opposite councils that barked mordantly enough — the Lateran ones above all, and other brickish assemblies they claimed as their own.

So too the most famous men of our own age, sharers in that excellent Reformation won by God's grace, have laid the same necessity out at length: among those specially called Reformed, the great Hottinger (ὁ πάνυ), in Ecclesiastical History Parts V–VI and in the Historico-Theological Analecta, Dissertation I, pages 1–82; among other Evangelicals, after Chytraeus and Celestine in the openings of their Augsburg-Confession histories, the illustrious Seckendorf in Lutheranism defended against Maimbourg, Baclerus in the Memorial of sixteenth-century affairs (p. 263 ff.), and most recently the celebrated Ulm divine Elias Viel in a special treatise.
100: Yet the Reformation itself had already been growing in secret for many ages — Flacius's Catalog of Witnesses of the Truth and James Ussher of Armagh in his golden booklet on church succession have said much about that hidden work.
Under God's lead it broke into the open in upper and lower Germany through Ulrich Zwingli and Martin Luther.
Zwingli led first by public teaching and by thundering against papal doctrine; Luther led first by striking the same targets with public writings and deeds of many kinds.

What chiefly dragged both men into the fight was the shameless papal indulgence-market, midwifed in one place by a certain Samsonius and in the other by infamous Tetzel (Gerhard Theodor Mejer, History of Religion, ch. V, §29, pp. 253–254).
101: §. II. Tetzel grew wilder still in our own Viadrina, selling under Conrad Wimpina's shield — Wimpina being the Academy's first Rector.

He hawked his wares and praised them once laid out: pay even ten shillings and receive absolution from any crime; drop a coin in the chest and souls leave Purgatory at once; buy pardon even if, by impossibles, you had violated God's Mother (Luther's Letter to Archbishop Albert of Brandenburg of Mainz, Jena Latin Tom. I, fol. 2).
That fury only hardened Luther's counterblow: at Wittenberg he had his Theses against the foul trade nailed to the church doors.
102: Pope Leo answered Luther's several most humble apologies and protests (Jena Latin Tom. I, fol. 69 end; fol. 192 and 210 end; finally fol. 435) with still harsher injustice and with teeth worthy of his name.
When that leonine message came, Luther burned the condemning Bull and lodged his appeal with Emperor Charles V (Wittenberg Latin Tom. II, fol. 44–45).
103: §. III. That clash brought imperial summons: in 1521 Charles V called Luther to Worms under safe-conduct and demanded a retractation.
Luther would not recant without first hearing his errors proved from Holy Scripture — and he held that line without wavering.

Meanwhile Frederick the Wise, Duke and Elector of Saxony, together with some other Romano-German estates, had drawn nearer to Luther's teaching. The same Emperor then set the Augsburg Diet for July 1530; Luther waited out the danger at Coburg, as Sleidan tells in Book VII.
From that Diet the blessed Spanheim, in his Elenchus, takes the title for certain chief Controversies with the so-called Augsburg-Confession theologians — the very Controversies we are to treat here.
Here the Hexades Prooemium ends; Annotatio I on the Augsburg Confession and its theologians follows.
